examples: The new dam [[checked]] the floods that had destroyed the lower valley every spring.
Each branch of government is meant to [[check]] the power of the others.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Foresters who inspected the burned hillside found that the fire break had [[checked]] the blaze: the flames reached the cleared strip and went no farther.
nearly.clue: the flames reached the cleared strip and went no farther

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The framers of the Constitution wanted each branch of government to [[check]] the others, so that no single official could gather too much power.
nearly.clue: so that no single official could gather too much power

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Clara opened her mouth to answer the insult, then [[checked]] herself, remembering that her mother was watching from the porch.
nearly.clue: remembering that her mother was watching from the porch

partners: check the spread / check one's anger / checks and balances

lookalikes.tell: Check means hold back; checkered means marked by ups and downs, as in a checkered past.

meaning: To reveal something without meaning to, such as a feeling, a secret or an origin.
examples: Her calm voice [[betrayed]] none of the fear she felt.
The slight tremor in his hands [[betrayed]] how nervous he was.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Though he swore loyalty to the duke, the steward's glance toward the door [[betrayed]] his wish to be gone.
nearly.clue: his wish to be gone

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The ice core looked uniform to the eye, but its chemistry [[betrayed]] a sudden warming about 12,000 years ago, when the levels of certain isotopes jumped within a few decades.
nearly.clue: when the levels of certain isotopes jumped within a few decades

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The spy never confessed, but the notes sewn into his coat [[betrayed]] his true purpose in the capital.
nearly.clue: the notes sewn into his coat

lookalikes.tell: Betray means reveal without meaning to; portray means depict on purpose.

meaning: To weaken something or expose it to danger, such as safety, health, principles or a reputation.
everyday: reach an agreement by giving ground
examples: A single leaked password can [[compromise]] an entire computer network.
The judge withdrew from the case rather than [[compromise]] the court's reputation for fairness.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The negotiators agreed on a smaller budget, but the cuts [[compromised]] the study itself: with half as many sensors, the team could no longer detect small earthquakes.
nearly.clue: the team could no longer detect small earthquakes

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The senator refused to meet the lobbyists halfway, fearing that any deal would [[compromise]] his standing with the voters who had elected him to oppose them.
nearly.clue: his standing with the voters who had elected him to oppose them

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Elizabeth would not accept the gift, for she knew that taking it would [[compromise]] her independence and leave her in Mr. Hart's debt.
nearly.clue: leave her in Mr. Hart's debt

lookalikes.tell: Compromise means weaken or settle by give-and-take; comprise means consist of.

meaning: To settle a disagreement by having each side give up part of what it wants.
examples: The two states [[compromised]] on the border, each taking half of the disputed valley.
After weeks of argument, the committee [[compromised]]: the library would open on Sundays, but only in the afternoon.
partners: compromise on terms / reach a compromise

lookalikes.tell: Compromise means settle by give-and-take; comprise means consist of.

meaning: To think about an idea or possibility, or to be willing to consider it.
examples: The board refused even to [[entertain]] the proposal to move the company's headquarters.
Few scientists in 1900 [[entertained]] the idea that continents could move.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The traveling players tried every trick to amuse the old king, but he would [[entertain]] no request to let them stay the winter.
nearly.clue: no request to let them stay the winter

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: For years, many geologists would not seriously [[entertain]] the theory that an asteroid killed the dinosaurs; only the discovery of a buried crater of the right age in Mexico changed their minds.
nearly.clue: only the discovery of a buried crater of the right age in Mexico changed their minds

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The general's advisers urged him to [[entertain]] the enemy's offer of a truce, arguing that his exhausted army could not survive another winter campaign.
nearly.clue: arguing that his exhausted army could not survive another winter campaign

partners: entertain an idea / a possibility / an offer

lookalikes.tell: Entertain means consider an idea; entreat means beg someone earnestly.

meaning: Very serious and worrying, or solemn in manner.
examples: The report warned of [[grave]] risks to the town's water supply.
The doctor's [[grave]] expression told the family everything before she spoke.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The general knew that retreating across the river would put his army in [[grave]] danger, since the enemy's cannon commanded both banks.
nearly.clue: since the enemy's cannon commanded both banks

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Epidemiologists considered the outbreak [[grave]]: the virus was spreading quickly, and no vaccine yet existed.
nearly.clue: the virus was spreading quickly, and no vaccine yet existed

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Standing at the churchyard gate, the vicar spoke in a [[grave]] voice of the harvest that had failed and the hard winter to come.
nearly.clue: of the harvest that had failed and the hard winter to come

partners: grave danger / concern / a grave mistake

lookalikes.tell: Grave means very serious; gravelly describes a rough, harsh voice.

meaning: To suggest or hint at something indirectly, without stating it.
examples: In her letter, the duchess [[intimated]] that she might support the marriage, though she never said so outright.
The mayor [[intimated]] that more layoffs were coming.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The two sisters had always been close, so Jane noticed at once when Mary [[intimated]], in the lightest possible tone, that she might not come home for Christmas.
nearly.clue: in the lightest possible tone

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The ambassador never threatened war directly; he merely [[intimated]] that his government's patience had limits.
nearly.clue: never threatened war directly; he merely

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The early data [[intimated]] that the treatment might work, but the researchers were careful not to claim more until the full trial was complete.
nearly.clue: careful not to claim more until the full trial was complete

lookalikes.tell: Intimate means hint; intimidate means frighten someone into doing something.

meaning: A goal or aim that someone works to reach.
examples: The expedition's main [[objective]] was to map the river's source.
Reducing traffic deaths became the city's chief [[objective]].

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The study's authors took pains to be unbiased, and their stated [[objective]] was simple: to measure how much plastic the river carried to the sea each year.
nearly.clue: was simple: to measure how much plastic the river carried

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Capturing the capital was never the rebels' [[objective]]; they wanted only to force the king to reopen the ports.
nearly.clue: they wanted only to force the king to reopen the ports

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Dalton's single [[objective]] that winter was to see at least one of her daughters married before spring.
nearly.clue: to see at least one of her daughters married before spring

partners: the main objective / achieve an objective

lookalikes.tell: An objective is a goal; an objection is a reason given against something.

meaning: Not well known; not famous.
examples: The song was written by an [[obscure]] composer whose name appears in no other record.
Darwin drew on the work of [[obscure]] naturalists as well as famous ones.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The poems of an [[obscure]] village schoolteacher, unknown outside her county during her lifetime, are now taught in universities.
nearly.clue: unknown outside her county during her lifetime

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The fungus had been described only once, in an [[obscure]] Dutch journal that few biologists had heard of, and it was then forgotten for a century.
nearly.clue: that few biologists had heard of

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The treaty was drafted not by the famous statesmen whose names it bears but by an [[obscure]] clerk, whose role came to light only in 1962.
nearly.clue: whose role came to light only in 1962

lookalikes.tell: Obscure here means little known; abstruse means hard to understand.

meaning: To cause or bring about something.
examples: The new tax [[occasioned]] widespread protest among merchants.
Her remark [[occasioned]] a long silence at the dinner table.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The king's birthday was meant to be a joyful day, but the tax he announced at the celebration [[occasioned]] riots in three cities.
nearly.clue: riots in three cities

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Doctors at first could not tell what had [[occasioned]] the patient's sudden fever; tests later traced it to a tick bite.
nearly.clue: tests later traced it to a tick bite

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Nothing in the letter itself could have [[occasioned]] such grief, her friends agreed, so the widow must have been weeping for something else.
nearly.clue: must have been weeping for something else

lookalikes.tell: Occasion as a verb means cause; occasional means happening now and then.

meaning: Ordinary and uninspired; lacking imagination or excitement.
examples: Critics called the film's plot [[pedestrian]], though they admired its photography.
Her early poems are [[pedestrian]]; only in her forties did she find her voice.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The novelist's descriptions of busy city streets, crowded with walkers and carriages, are vivid enough, but his dialogue is [[pedestrian]], and every character sounds the same.
nearly.clue: every character sounds the same

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The grant committee dismissed the proposal to count foot traffic on city sidewalks as [[pedestrian]]; it wanted bolder, more original research.
nearly.clue: it wanted bolder, more original research

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Historians once dismissed the diary as [[pedestrian]], a dull record of weather and prices, until they realized how much those prices revealed about the war's effects.
nearly.clue: a dull record of weather and prices

lookalikes.tell: Pedestrian means dull (or on foot); pediatric means relating to children's medicine.

meaning: To think carefully and seriously about something, often something in the past; usually used as “reflect on.”
everyday: throw back light or an image
examples: In her memoir, she [[reflects]] on the choices that led her away from medicine.
The long voyage gave him time to [[reflect]] on his failures.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Sitting beside the still lake, whose surface mirrored the pines, Ellen [[reflected]] on how little her life had changed in ten years.
nearly.clue: on how little her life had changed in ten years

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: After the telescope's main mirror was found to be flawed, the engineers [[reflected]] on what had gone wrong, and their report became a guide for later missions.
nearly.clue: on what had gone wrong

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Late in life, the former president [[reflected]] on the war with regret, writing that he had trusted his generals too readily.
nearly.clue: writing that he had trusted his generals too readily

partners: reflect on the past / reflect that

lookalikes.tell: Reflect on means think carefully about; deflect means turn something aside.

meaning: A doubt or concern that keeps someone from fully accepting or supporting something.
everyday: a booking, as for a room or a table
examples: Several senators voted for the bill despite [[reservations]] about its cost.
She accepted the job without [[reservation]].

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mr. Grey had booked the finest rooms at the inn for their anniversary, yet his wife confessed one [[reservation]]: she feared the journey would be too much for her mother.
nearly.clue: she feared the journey would be too much for her mother

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The committee approved the new drug, but two members recorded [[reservations]], noting that the trial had not included any patients over seventy.
nearly.clue: noting that the trial had not included any patients over seventy

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Although he urged the delegates to sign the Constitution, Franklin admitted [[reservations]], confessing that there were several parts of it he did not at present approve.
nearly.clue: several parts of it he did not at present approve

lookalikes.tell: A reservation here is a doubt; a reservoir is a store of water.

meaning: Based on good reasoning or evidence; reliable and sensible.
examples: The engineers found the bridge's design structurally [[sound]].
Her argument is [[sound]], but it rests on data that are twenty years old.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The lab's recordings of whale calls were loud and clear, but were its conclusions [[sound]]? Two independent teams, repeating the analysis, reached the same result.
nearly.clue: Two independent teams, repeating the analysis, reached the same result

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Critics mocked the plan for a canal across the isthmus, but the surveyor's reasoning was [[sound]]: the route he chose avoided the mountains entirely.
nearly.clue: the route he chose avoided the mountains entirely

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mr. Knox gave his nephew advice that was [[sound]], if unwelcome: to sell the failing farm while it still had buyers.
nearly.clue: to sell the failing farm while it still had buyers

lookalikes.tell: Sound here means well reasoned; resound means echo loudly.

meaning: Plain and simple, with nothing extra; lean and economical in style.
examples: Hemingway's [[spare]] prose leaves much of the story unsaid.
The room was [[spare]]: a bed, a chair and a single window.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Unlike the ornate novels of her day, Moore's stories are written in [[spare]] sentences, rarely longer than ten words and almost free of adjectives.
nearly.clue: rarely longer than ten words and almost free of adjectives

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The Shakers built [[spare]] furniture, with clean lines and no carving, because they regarded decoration as a form of pride.
nearly.clue: with clean lines and no carving

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The architect's design for the polar research station was [[spare]]: a single steel box with nothing inside but lab benches and bunks.
nearly.clue: nothing inside but lab benches and bunks

lookalikes.tell: Spare means plain and lean in style; sparse means thinly spread or scattered.

meaning: To make someone or something undergo or be exposed to something, often something unpleasant; used as “subject to.”
everyday: make into a topic of study
examples: The samples were [[subjected]] to temperatures of more than 1,000 degrees.
The prisoners were [[subjected]] to months of questioning.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: For her chemistry project, Lena [[subjected]] ordinary tap water to a series of tests, measuring its lead, chlorine and iron.
nearly.clue: to a series of tests

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The new law [[subjected]] every imported book to inspection by a royal censor, who could order any volume burned.
nearly.clue: who could order any volume burned

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Aunt Ruth [[subjected]] every visitor to a long account of her ailments, and few visitors came twice.
nearly.clue: and few visitors came twice

partners: subject to scrutiny / to tests / to criticism

lookalikes.tell: Subject someone to something means make them undergo it; subjugate means conquer and control.

meaning: Lacking something needed, or not good enough; often used as “found wanting.”
examples: When the storm came, the town's emergency plans were found [[wanting]].
The report was thorough in its data but [[wanting]] in explanation.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The colonists had wanted a strong army for years, but when war came, their militia was found [[wanting]]: poorly trained, it scattered at the first volley.
nearly.clue: poorly trained, it scattered at the first volley

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Newton's theory explained the planets' orbits remarkably well, but it was [[wanting]] in one respect: it could not fully account for the slow shift in Mercury's orbit.
nearly.clue: it could not fully account for the slow shift in Mercury's orbit

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Kind and generous as he was, Mr. Pell was sadly [[wanting]] in common sense, and his family's fortune dwindled with each of his schemes.
nearly.clue: his family's fortune dwindled with each of his schemes

lookalikes.tell: Wanting means lacking; wanton means reckless or deliberately cruel.

meaning: The period or situation that follows an important event; usually used as “in the wake of.”
examples: In the [[wake]] of the scandal, the company replaced its entire board.
New safety laws followed in the [[wake]] of the factory fire.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The 1906 earthquake struck before dawn, jolting San Francisco from sleep. In its [[wake]], the city built a separate high-pressure water system so that firefighters would never again run dry.
nearly.clue: the city built a separate high-pressure water system

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: In the [[wake]] of the oil spill, biologists counted seabirds along the coast every month for five years to measure the damage.
nearly.clue: counted seabirds along the coast every month for five years

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Nobody in the house slept well that night; in the [[wake]] of their father's announcement, the children lay whispering about what the move would mean.
nearly.clue: of their father's announcement

partners: in the wake of a disaster / a decision

lookalikes.tell: In the wake of means following an event; awake means not asleep.

meaning: To put forward an idea, theory or claim for others to consider.
examples: In 1912 Alfred Wegener [[advanced]] the theory that the continents had once been joined.
In the appeal, the lawyer [[advanced]] an argument the trial court had never heard.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Glaciers were known to move, but it was Louis Agassiz who most forcefully [[advanced]] the idea that ice sheets had once covered much of northern Europe.
nearly.clue: the idea that ice sheets had once covered much of northern Europe

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: As the army marched forward, one of its officers [[advanced]] a daring proposal: to cross the river at night and attack from the rear.
nearly.clue: a daring proposal

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: At dinner, Mr. Ward [[advanced]] the opinion that novels were ruining young minds, and his niece, who had three hidden in her room, said nothing.
nearly.clue: the opinion that novels were ruining young minds

partners: advance a theory / an argument / a claim

lookalikes.tell: Advance an idea means put it forward; advocate an idea means argue hard for it.

meaning: To express an opinion or complaint openly, so that others hear it.
examples: At the town meeting, residents [[aired]] their concerns about the new highway.
The two partners agreed to [[air]] their disagreements in private, not in the press.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Residents worried about the air near the plant finally [[aired]] their complaints at a public hearing, where engineers presented new pollution data.
nearly.clue: their complaints at a public hearing

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: For years, the workers' grievances had been whispered in the mill yard; the strike of 1912 [[aired]] them before the whole nation.
nearly.clue: before the whole nation

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Lowe threw open the parlor windows, then [[aired]] her opinion of her son's new friends, at length and in a voice the neighbors could hear.
nearly.clue: her opinion of her son's new friends

lookalikes.tell: Air means express openly; err means make a mistake.

meaning: To invent a new word or phrase.
examples: The German zoologist Ernst Haeckel [[coined]] the word “ecology” in 1866.
A reporter [[coined]] the phrase “Dust Bowl” to describe the drought-stricken plains.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The Treasury had just begun to mint a new silver dollar when a newspaper editor [[coined]] a nickname for it that stuck for decades.
nearly.clue: a nickname for it that stuck for decades

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The astronomer Fred Hoyle, who doubted the theory, is said to have [[coined]] the term “Big Bang” during a 1949 radio broadcast.
nearly.clue: the term “Big Bang”

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Dickens so often [[coined]] memorable names for his characters that some, such as “scrooge,” became ordinary English words.
nearly.clue: became ordinary English words

partners: coin a term / a phrase / a word

lookalikes.tell: Coin a word means invent it; cite a word means quote someone else's use of it.

meaning: To become smaller, shorter or narrower.
examples: Metal rails [[contract]] in cold weather, which is why builders leave small gaps between them.
The economy [[contracted]] for three straight quarters.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Engineers working under a government agreement found that the new alloy [[contracts]] far less than steel in extreme cold, so bridges built from it need smaller expansion joints.
nearly.clue: so bridges built from it need smaller expansion joints

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: After the treaty was signed, the empire's borders [[contracted]] sharply, and within a decade it held barely half the territory it had ruled at its height.
nearly.clue: held barely half the territory

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: As the winter deepened, the family's world [[contracted]] to a single warm room, where they ate, slept and read aloud by the stove.
nearly.clue: to a single warm room

lookalikes.tell: Contract means shrink or make a formal agreement; contact means touch or get in touch with.

meaning: To catch or develop an illness.
examples: Many of the canal workers [[contracted]] malaria in the swamps along the route.
Travelers who drank from the well often [[contracted]] cholera within days.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The workers who signed on to build the railroad expected hard labor and low pay; few expected that one in five would [[contract]] yellow fever before the line was finished.
nearly.clue: yellow fever before the line was finished

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Bats can carry the virus without becoming sick, but people who [[contract]] it from them may develop a high fever within a week.
nearly.clue: may develop a high fever within a week

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Having agreed to tutor the Morland children for a year, Miss Hale [[contracted]] a fever in her first month and spent the rest of the winter in bed.
nearly.clue: a fever in her first month

lookalikes.tell: Contract an illness means catch it; contact means touch, which is often how an illness spreads.

meaning: To express something in a particular kind of language or style; usually used as “couched in.”
examples: The ultimatum was [[couched]] in polite language, but its meaning was unmistakable.
Scientists often [[couch]] their boldest claims in cautious terms.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Resting on a couch in his sickroom, the old king dictated a reply to the rebels that was [[couched]] in the gentlest terms, yet refused every one of their demands.
nearly.clue: in the gentlest terms, yet refused every one of their demands

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The report's warning was [[couched]] in such technical language that few lawmakers understood how serious the danger was.
nearly.clue: in such technical language

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Her refusal, [[couched]] in so many compliments that he took it at first for an acceptance, left Mr. Crane bewildered.
nearly.clue: in so many compliments that he took it at first for an acceptance

lookalikes.tell: Couched in means expressed in; crouch means bend low to the ground.
